summary: Add proof-step practice and an official-specification example to strengthen the four induction settings.

improvements.why: Most existing non-structured items only calculate a value from an already proved formula; learners need to construct the induction step.
improvements.what: Add one exam-style Prove or Show that item in each setting, using fresh expressions: a summation requiring the next summand, a divisibility claim requiring an integer quotient, a recurrence requiring substitution of $u_k$, and a non-triangular matrix power requiring all four entries. Avoid duplicating the four existing structured proofs.

improvements.why: The four existing faded versions ask only for numerical evaluation, so none rehearses a partially completed proof.
improvements.what: Add one worked proof with a faded version whose blank starts at the key $k$ to $k+1$ transition and whose answer checks the resulting expression; retain all existing worked examples.

improvements.where: note, after the divisibility worked example
improvements.why: Pearson's official FP1 8.1 guidance uses $3^{2n}+11$ divisible by $4$, a distinct divisibility form absent from the chapter; its teaching guidance says divisibility is typically the most challenging induction setting.
improvements.what: Add a concise second divisibility transition for $3^{2n}+11$: from $3^{2k}+11=4q$, derive $3^{2(k+1)}+11=9(3^{2k}+11)-88=4(9q-22)$, and explicitly identify the integer quotient. Paraphrase the sources.

improvements.why: The learner's revision guide highlights the final conclusion as a mark-bearing step; the current note gives a general reminder but no reusable sentence for an arbitrary start index.
improvements.what: Add a short model conclusion: having verified $P(n_0)$ and proved $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$ for arbitrary $k\geq n_0$, conclude $P(n)$ for all integers $n\geq n_0$.
